title: IPVS + conntrack surge causing scheduler thundering-herd — incident notes and mitigations
content:
Summary:
We observed a cluster-wide client connection surge to IPVS-backed services that correlated with a sharp conntrack table growth on most worker nodes. The kernel began dropping new connections, kube-proxy saw timeouts, pods became Pending due to scheduler retries and eventual pod churn. Effect: brief but high tail-latency for user requests (~30-90s), increased API-server request queue, and transient node pressure (netdev queue growth) that triggered kubelet eviction churn on 4 nodes.

High-level hypothesis:
A burst of external traffic (large number of short-lived connections) exposed a config and capacity mismatch: conntrack table and IPVS connlimit defaults + kube-proxy sync loop timing caused kernel connection drops and increased kube-proxy CPU. The scheduler reacted to pod readiness failures and created a thundering herd of scheduling attempts for the same pods, exacerbating apiserver pressure.

Detection timeline (UTC):
- 2025-11-02 09:17: alert: "Service errors > 5xx" firing from synthetic checks (frontend-healthcheck)
- 09:18: spikes in iptable/ipvs sync latency (kube-proxy) visible in node-metrics dashboard
- 09:19: conntrack entries per node increased from 1.2k -> 85k (rate: ~8k/min)
- 09:20: network transmit queue length on nodes A,B,C,D jumped; packet drops observed on dmesg (NET_RX drop warnings)
- 09:22: pods stuck Pending with error: "insufficient resources" (ephemeral due to kubelet resource accounting flapping)
- 09:25: remediation action: temporarily scale down the frontend ingress replicas to reduce new connection pressure
- 09:30: conntrack growth slowed; errors declined; full recovery by 09:42

What we saw in logs / metrics (snippets):
- node dmesg excerpt: "[kernel] nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet"
- kube-proxy metrics: ipvs_sync_duration_seconds_bucket high tail values at 0.9s+
- kubelet logs: repeated pod admission failures while API server load high (timeouts on endpoints update)

Immediate mitigations taken during the incident (what worked):
1) Scale-down: reduced ingress/frontend replicas from 20 -> 6 over 09:25-09:27 to reduce new TCP connection rate. This immediately lowered conntrack creation rate.
2) Bumped kube-proxy concurrency (temporary heap): set KUBE_PROXY_EXTRA_ARGS=--sync-period=10s -> 2s on a small canary pool to test effect. This reduced ipvs sync latency for that canary, but increased kube-proxy CPU; not rolled cluster-wide.
3) Conntrack garbage collect: ran conntrack -D on two most affected nodes (manual) -> helped speed reclaim but is risky; did with caution.
4) Short-term IPVS scheduling fallback: enabled service session affinity mode to "none" for one high-cardinality service to reduce per-connection state.

Why these helped: scale-down reduced input rate; conntrack flush reclaimed table entries; smaller sync period on kube-proxy reduced ipvs reconciliation tail latency on canary nodes, demonstrating that kube-proxy scheduling can be a contributor to observed sync spikes.

Root cause analysis (current understanding):
- Trigger: short-lived client workload burst from a partner integration (see linked Slack trace) generating many 1-3s TCP connections per client.
- Kernel/conntrack: default nf_conntrack_max and hashsize were sized for steady-state common loads but not for sudden bursts with thousands of concurrent flows per node. Table hits the limit -> kernel drops -> connection errors visible at application layer.
- kube-proxy + IPVS: under high conn churn, ipvs sync loop takes longer; kube-proxy CPU increases which slows reconciliation (endpoints update cycles), amplifying the surface of inconsistency between IPVS tables and apiserver view.
- Scheduler amplification: controllers saw failed readiness and attempted recreate/reschedule; many pods in short window produced scheduling queue thrash. This created apiserver pressure (high list/watch churn), contributing to overall recovery slowness.

Non-root contributing factors (observed):
- No automatic conntrack autoscaling and no node-level alerting tied specifically to conntrack table fill rate (we had only aggregate network errors alerting).
- Service patterns: some services opened per-request ephemeral connections to backend pods rather than reusing keepalive.
- kube-proxy default sync-period larger in some clusters -> longer reconciliation tail.

Immediate follow-ups / action items (owners and rough ETA):
- SRE: Add conntrack-specific alert (conntrack table > 70% of nf_conntrack_max) and alert playbook. ETA: 2 days (owner: Sophie Nguyen).
- Platform: Raise default nf_conntrack_max on worker nodes from 131072 -> 524288 for production pools where traffic volatility is expected. Validate memory/CPU impact. ETA: 1 week (owner: Luis Martinez).
- Platform: Document and automate safe conntrack flush playbook (when and how to run conntrack -D) and add a runbook step to query conntrack metrics pre-flush. ETA: 4 days (owner: Daniel Kim).
- App Eng: Investigate long-tail clients that create per-request TCP connections; add keep-alive or connection pooling in partner integration. ETA: 2 weeks (owner: Product Team Lead assigned in JIRA-SRE-1429).
- SRE: Investigate kube-proxy tuning: evaluate reduced sync-period vs CPU cost tradeoff and create a canary pattern. ETA: 2 weeks (owner: SRE kernel/network area).
- Product/Platform: Add graceful scheduling backoff to controller reconcilers when transient node pressure is detected to avoid immediate reschedule churn. ETA: 3 weeks (owner: Platform Eng).

Longer-term mitigations to prevent recurrence:
- Conntrack autoscaling heuristics: build node-level logic (kubelet or systemd hook) to increase nf_conntrack_max when node memory and conntrack hash overhead allow.
- Prefer keepalive by default in client libraries and enforce in partner contract; instrument per-service connection churn metrics.
- Replace manual conntrack flush with safe rolling reclaim approach integrated into rollout automation with pre-checks.
- Improve kube-proxy metrics: expose ipvs table length and reconcile counters to narrow detection window. Consider moving to a dual-proxy or eBPF-based datapath in long run.

Outstanding questions / unknowns:
- Exact request pattern from partner: need more precise sample logs from partner (SRE-1429).
- Does nf_conntrack_max increase create unacceptable memory pressure on the smallest worker type? Need benchmarking.
- What is the long-term tradeoff of aggressive kube-proxy sync vs CPU vs stability?

Post-incident timeline & comms:
- 2025-11-02 10:10: internal incident update sent to #sre (brief summary + mitigation)
- 2025-11-02 12:00: notified partner CS/eng to request review of client behavior and fix connection pooling
- 2025-11-05: scheduled deep-dive with app team and platform to agree on next steps (conntrack default change and client keepalive requirement)

Appendix: quick commands used during triage (for runbook integration)
- conntrack -S                 # show conntrack stats
- sudo conntrack -L | wc -l    # list-count (expensive)
- sudo conntrack -D            # flush (dangerous: disrupts active sessions)
- ss -s                       # socket statistics summary
- watch -n1 cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
- journalctl -k -b | grep conntrack

Runbook draft (short play):
- Detection: alert fires (conntrack > 70% or ipvs_sync_latency > 1s) -> escalate to on-call SRE.
- Triage quick checks (5-10m): check conntrack stats; verify if traffic surge external or internal; identify top 10 source IPs by conntrack entries.
- Mitigation order: 1) Reduce ingress/new connection rate (scale down replicas or throttle via ingress rate limit), 2) If safe, apply targeted conntrack flush on 1-2 worst nodes with controlled window, 3) Consider temporary session-affinity disable for high-cardinality services, 4) If API-server pressure high, pause controller loops (last resort) to reduce scheduling churn.
- Recovery: wait for conntrack free to drop under threshold and ipvs sync latency to return to baseline, then roll-up scaling gradually.

Notes & learning (informal):
- This incident reminded us that kernel-level limits still matter for cloud-native infra; it's easy to assume K8s handles ephemeral scale but Linux conntrack is a hard chokepoint.
- We should treat `conntrack` metrics like any other infra quota (SLOs and alerting) rather than ad-hoc monitoring.
- Consider an experiment with eBPF-based service mesh datapath for high-churn workloads.

Status: doc is a working draft for the incident review — seeking engineering + app-team feedback before turning into a short incident postmortem and a platform change PR.
